title: Prompt synthesis field diary
content:
Goal: lightweight, reusable micro-templates for robust instruction-following under tight token budgets. This is a working notebook — notes, quick experiments, and hypotheses. Not polished; for my eyes + Maya/Evan.

Top-level idea
- Compose prompts from small orthogonal building blocks: role header, goal-statement, constraint-block, exemplar-suite, negative-examples, output-format. Keep each block < 128 tokens when possible.
- Aim for graceful degradation: if context truncated, older blocks can be dropped in a defined order (negative-examples > exemplar-suite > constraint-block > role header).
- Try to get consistent terse JSON outputs for downstream parsing.

Quick heuristics discovered (observational)
1) Anchoring the output with an explicit "schema" line (one short JSON example) massively stabilizes structure even when model is otherwise verbose.
2) Negative instructions ("Do NOT invent facts") are helpful but can be noisy; placing them before examples reduces hallucinations more than after examples.
3) Short, high-quality exemplars beat longer, noisy exemplars in low-token regimes (< 256 tokens).

Experiment A: 3-shot micro-template (target: Q->concise JSON)
Template (block ordering):
- Role: "You are a concise assistant."
- Goal: "For each question, produce {answer, rationale_summary} in JSON."
- Constraints: "max_tokens=80; avoid invented dates; prefer 'unknown' to guessing."
- Schema: single-line example: {"answer":"...","rationale_summary":"..."}
- Exemplars: three short Q/A pairs

Exemplars used:
1) Q: "When was the Magna Carta signed?" A: {"answer":"1215","rationale_summary":"barons forced King John to agree to terms at Runnymede"}
2) Q: "Define polymorphism in OOP." A: {"answer":"objects sharing interface for multiple types","rationale_summary":"allows same code to operate on different object types"}
3) Q: "What is the capital of canada?" A: {"answer":"Ottawa","rationale_summary":"federal capital, established as compromise between rivals"}

Results (redwood-v1-small, temp=0.0):
- Mostly correct, but capitalization varies ("canada" -> "Canada" correct). Rationale sometimes expanded beyond summary length. JSON well-formed 92% of runs.

Failure case observed:
- When input is long or includes irrelevant URL, model drops constraints and returns prose instead of JSON.
- Token truncation tends to remove exemplar 3 first (unexpected behavior vs our drop order).

Notes: try moving schema to the very end (post-examples) in next run — hypothesis: schema later acts as immediate post-prompt anchor.

Experiment B: negative-example priming
- Add a short negative-example block: "Bad: {"answer":"Paris", "rationale_summary":"made up"}  // example of hallucinated answer"
- Position: between constraints and schema

Observed:
- Hallucinations reduced ~30% on QA where model previously asserted plausible but false dates.
- However, some runs mimic the phrasing of the negative example (rarely flips and outputs the bad example structure as answer). Add explicit 'Do not output the following as answer' preface.

Edge cases worth cataloging
- Numeric fuzziness: models invent years with high confidence (-> add 'if unsure, respond "unknown"')
- Ambiguous named-entities: model invents organization locations when prompter uses partial names. Put clarifying follow-up question template.
- Temporal references: 'recent' causes model to guess; include anchor like 'as of 2024-01-01'.

Micro-pattern: "progressive specificity"
- Start general, then restrict. Example: role -> goal -> constraints -> schema -> exemplars -> final instruction
- If we flip exemplars earlier, we see better stylistic mimicry but more hallucination. Tradeoff: style vs factual conservatism.

Bench notes and metrics
- Test harness: 300 synthetic Qs (mix factual / commonsense / open-ended), evaluate: JSON-validity, exact-answer-match (for fact), hallucination-rate (annotated).
- Current baseline (v1-small, default prompt): JSON-valid 78%, hallucination 18%.
- Micro-template (above): JSON-valid 92%, hallucination 10%, but recall drops slightly on obscure facts.

Quick TODOs
- [ ] Run same micro-template with redwood-v1-quant4 and redwood-v2-medium.
- [ ] Add explicit fallback message when nothing confident: output {"answer":"unknown","confidence":0}
- [ ] Implement deterministic exemplar drop order in harness (so truncation behavior reproducible) — GH-PR #102
- [ ] Try schema-last variant (move schema after exemplars) and compare stability.

Rough few-shot sets to try next week (ideas)
- Contrasting pair set: for each Q, show one correct and one subtly incorrect exemplar to bias conservative outputs.
- Negative-first set: lead with multiple negative examples to see if it reduces hallucination more.
- Style-locked set: exemplars that all use passive voice / specific vocabulary to encourage output style.

Loose meta-notes
- This directory is my low-friction lab notebook for prompt wiring. Expect typos. Shareable to Evan/Maya but not polished for docs.
- When we move promising candidates to product, create a 'canonical templates' page in Confluence and a small test suite in github/prompt-harness.

References + links (internal)
- Slack thread: #prompt-playground — see thread on 2024-11-22 (Maya flagged schema anchoring)
- JIRA: JIRA-ML-2345 (prompt stability experiments)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-harness/pulls/102 (deterministic drop order)

Random scratch ideas (brain dump)
- 'micro-guardian' block: a 1-sentence validator appended to prompt: "If output is not valid JSON or violates constraints, respond simply: {"error":"validation_failed"}" — could help downstream parsers.
- 'confidence slider' hint: "Prefer shorter answers; mark confidence 0-1" to calibrate length.

End of entry: 2025-02-14. Next update: run quant4 sweep and add metric table.
